It depends on exactly what you mean by "scramble/pixelate" it. This is fundamentally just a basic crypto question.

There are algorithms that enable you to go from A to B, but not from B to A, while maintaining all the data. This is how public key cryptography works. Somebody publishes their public key. You encrypt your message A to B using that public key, and publish B. Now the person who owns public key takes message B and is able to convert it to A using their private key. The public keys are, as per the name, public and can be freely shared. The only thing needs to be kept secret is the one private key. This should be very counter intuitive. The math there is not difficult, but fairly lengthy and doesn't have an easy tl/dr other than primes and modulos enable you to do counter intuitive stuff.

Hashes are another type of crypto that enable you to tell with a really good certainty that B probably came from A, but it is impossible to get from B to A since information is lost and it's possible (though extremely rare with a good hashing algorithm) that two different values could hash to the same result.

And then at the end there are simple ciphers. For instance a caesar cipher. This would be something where you just turn every red pixel green, every green pixel blue, and so on. As long as each pixel is converted to a distinct color, you could get from B to A trivially. These sort of algorithms, however, are no longer used for anything since they're trivial to crack. For instance one immediate strategy would be letter frequency. If some conversation being encrypted is 'normal' then you know that the most common symbol is very likely to be an "e". Interestingly enough they'd be perhaps even easier to crack for a picture than for text due to the fact that pixels that are close to each other tend to have very similar values. You'd need some sort of decent image recognition AI to test the values, but you'd likely be able to converge on something very close to the original picture extremely quickly.
